title: Steady a swinging plumb bob, then pencil-mark the worktop under its point: the spot directly below a hole in a shelf
instruction: Use the plumb bob to mark the worktop directly below the hole in the shelf: steady the swinging bob, let it hang free and still, make one pencil mark on the worktop under its point, and lift the pencil away.
context: Carpenters (O*NET 47-2031.00, 889,700 US workers: "Verify trueness of structure, using plumb bob and level") and plumbers and pipefitters (47-2152.00, 510,600: "Locate and mark the position of pipe installations, connections, passage holes, or fixtures in structures") carry a point straight down with a plumb bob, for example to mark where a pipe dropped through a shelf will meet the worktop. The bob shows that point only while it hangs free and still, and once hung it swings for minutes. So the worker stops the swing by hand, lets go without giving it a push, and marks under the point without touching bob or line. Everything here is full size: a standard 16 oz bob and the usual 18 in between a worktop and the shelf or wall unit above it. For a robot this is damping a pendulum by touch and then working in a 6 mm gap under a hanging weight that the lightest contact sets moving again.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table, which is the worktop (x forward, y left; heights above the worktop). (1) A wall shelf, fixed: 18 mm plywood, 30 cm wide (y), 20 cm deep (x), its underside 45.7 cm (18 in) up, front edge at x 26, centred on y 0, on an 18 mm plywood backboard 30 cm wide and 47.5 cm tall standing at x 46. A hole for the line 6 cm in from the front edge, at x 32, y 0. (2) A plumb line: 2 mm orange braided line through the hole, tied to a brass screw on the shelf's top, 33.1 cm long from the hole's lower edge to the bob. (3) A 16 oz (454 g) brass plumb bob on the line, 12 cm long: a 6 cm taper down to a steel point, a body 3.2 cm across and 4.5 cm long, a cap 1.6 cm across and 1.5 cm long. Hanging still, its point is 6 mm above the worktop over x 32, y 0. At the start it is at rest with its point 2 cm toward the arms (x 30), the line straight, and is let go as the trial starts: it swings 2 cm either side along x, once every 1.2 s. Left alone the swing halves in about 2 minutes. (4) A carpenter's pencil: flat, 15 x 7 mm, 17.5 cm long, 10 g, red, sharpened to a point over 2.5 cm. It lies on its wide face in a rest, sloping 50 degrees: its point down at x 24, y -19, 1.2 cm up; its other end at x 24, y -30.2, 14.6 cm up. (5) The pencil's rest, fixed, pine: a groove 16.5 mm wide and 11.7 cm long sloping at 50 degrees with a stop at its lower end, on a post and a foot plate 5 x 13 cm. Both arms start in the raised ready pose, grippers open. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Tools: a ruler, the trial video and two close-up cameras on the bob's point. P is the point on the worktop directly below the hole (where the settled bob points). A mark: the pencil marks only while its point is in contact with the worktop and pressed on it with 0.3 N or more (a light stroke, about 30 g on the point; on a bench, the graphite left on the paper); a point held just above the worktop or resting on it more lightly leaves nothing. A mark runs as far as the pressed point is dragged, until the point is lifted 4 mm; its distance is from P to its farthest part. Hanging free and still: the bob's point has stayed within 3 mm of plumb (measured across; on a bench, from two calibrated close-up views, one along x and one along y) for 1.5 s, with every part of both grippers' fingers and palms at least 2 cm clear of the bob and 3.6 cm from its line. A plumbed mark is one made while the bob was hanging free and still. At the end of the trial: 1.0 if there is at least one mark, every mark is plumbed and within 3 mm of P, the pencil's point is at least 4 mm off the worktop, and the bob is hanging free and still; 0.5 if a plumbed mark lies within 10 mm of P; 0.25 if the bob hung free and still at some time; else 0. The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s.
reset_notes: Rub the pencil mark off the worktop (or tape a fresh sheet of paper under the bob), put the pencil back in its rest, draw the bob 2 cm toward the arms on its taut line and let it go as the trial starts. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, PhysX at 240 Hz. The line is a stiff 2 mm rod hinged freely at the hole and the bob's cap: exact while the bob hangs. Joint damping makes the free swing halve in about 2 min (measured: 20 to 14 mm in 60 s). A mark needs contact and force: the pencil's lead rides a stiff spring (600 N/m, 1.5 mm travel) read as a force gauge, and dots are laid only while its point is on the worktop at 0.3 N or more (an estimate of a light stroke; a real lead is rigid). The hole is drawn, not cut.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (both grippers reached toward the swinging bob without closing on it; the bob was never steadied and no mark was made); demo: 1.0 (bob left within 0.2 mm of plumb, pencil pressed on with 0.49 N, mark 0.5 mm from the point, full score at step 680)
